title: Woodruff’s Comeback Shines: Secures Spot on Brewers’ World Series Roster After Remarkable Recovery
body:
Milwaukee’s veteran right‑hander Brandon Woodruff, who has battled injuries and a mid‑season slump, earned a place on the Brewers’ World Series roster on the eve of Game 1, cementing his status as the club’s longest‑tenured pitcher heading to the championship stage. The decision, confirmed during the team’s final pre‑game workout, underscores the Brewers’ confidence in Woodruff’s rebound and highlights the depth of a rotation that has shouldered a grueling postseason run.

Woodruff’s path to the series has been anything but smooth. The 28‑year‑old logged a career‑best 12 wins and a 2.86 ERA in 2023, but a lingering shoulder issue limited him to just five starts in the first half of 2024. After a painstaking rehabilitation program, he returned in late July and posted a 3.40 ERA over his last ten appearances, striking out 68 batters in 58 innings. His resurgence was capped by a dominant six‑inning, five‑strikeout effort in the NLDS Game 3 against the Arizona Diamondbacks, where he helped Milwaukee clinch the series with a 5‑2 victory. Those performances convinced manager Craig Counsell and baseball operations chief Matt Arnold that Woodruff’s health and recent form merit a roster spot, even as the club carries a healthy mix of younger arms.

The Brewers entered the World Series with a pitching staff that has been both resilient and versatile. Veteran left‑hander Corbin Burnes, who has anchored the rotation since 2020, remains the ace, while the emerging right‑hander Freddy Peralta, who logged a 2.76 ERA in the playoffs, provides a reliable third option. Reliever Trevor Cunningham, who has been a bullpen workhorse all season, is slated for the closer role. Adding Woodruff to the mix not only bolsters the starting depth but also offers a left‑right balance that could prove crucial in a series that may stretch to seven games. The decision also reflects a broader trend in modern baseball: teams are increasingly willing to trust veteran pitchers who have demonstrated durability and the ability to adapt after injury, rather than relying solely on younger, untested arms.

Analysts note that Woodruff’s inclusion sends a clear message to the opposition. The New York Yankees, Milwaukee’s opponents, will have to prepare for a right‑hander who can locate his fastball on the inside corner and generate late‑life movement on his slider. While his velocity has dipped slightly from the mid‑90s he once consistently hit, his command and pitch sequencing have improved, making him a more cerebral pitcher. “He’s not just throwing hard; he’s painting the corners and attacking hitters’ weaknesses,” said former Brewers pitcher and current ESPN analyst Jim Miller. “If he can stay healthy, he gives Milwaukee a third quality starter who can go deep into games, which is a luxury in a short series.”

The roster move also carries sentimental weight for the franchise and its fans. Woodruff, drafted in the fifth round of the 2015 MLB draft, has spent his entire professional career with Milwaukee, climbing from the rookie leagues to the big club in 2019. His perseverance through shoulder surgery in 2022 and a subsequent rehab stint in Triple‑A Nashville has endeared him to the Milwaukee faithful, who have watched his evolution from a promising prospect to a dependable frontline starter. By securing his spot on the World Series roster, the organization rewards both his on‑field contributions and his loyalty, reinforcing a culture that values homegrown talent.

Looking ahead, the Brewers will rely on Woodruff’s durability and experience as they navigate the high‑stakes environment of the Fall Classic. If he can replicate his late‑season form, he could log at least 20 innings across the series, providing much‑needed rest for the bullpen and allowing manager Counsell to manage the rotation with flexibility. Conversely, any setback could force Milwaukee to lean more heavily on its younger arms, testing the depth they have cultivated throughout the season. As the team prepares for the opening pitch on Friday night, all eyes will be on Woodruff’s first start, a moment that could define both his personal comeback narrative and the Brewers’ quest for their first championship since 1982.
